mcq.QUESTION_DESC: If the limits of an integral transform are from \((-\infty,+\infty) \)it is called:
In the convolution theorem, the Fourier transform of \(f(x) * g(x) =\)

sq.ANSWER:
• Lineraity property : \( F [af(x)+bg(x)] = aF [f(x)]+bF [g(x)]\)                      --- (1 m)
  • Shifting property :If \( F [f(x)] =F(s) , \) then \(F [f(x-a)] =e^{ias}F(s)\)              --- (1 m)
  • If \(F [f(x)] =F(s) , \) then \(F [e^{ias} f(x)]= F(s+a)\)                                           --- (1 m)
  • Change of scale property : If \( F [f(x)] =F(s) , \) then \(F [f(ax)] = \frac{1}{|a|} F(\frac {s}{a})\) where a \(\neq \) 0.   --- (1 m)
  • If \( F [f(x)] =F(s) , \)then \(F[ f(x) cos ax ] =\frac 1 2 [F(s -a)+F(s+a)]\)                    --- (1 m)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: List out the five properties of Fourier Transforms.

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Fourier transform: } F(s) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{i s x} dx\)

(3 Mark)

\(\text{Inverse: } f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(s) e^{-i s x} ds\)

(3 Mark)

\(\text{Conditions: } f(x) \text{ is piecewise continuous and absolutely integrable on } (-\infty, \infty)\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Define the Fourier transform of a function } f(x) \text{ and its inverse. State the conditions for existence.}\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Property: If } F[f(x)] = F(s) \text{ then } F[f(ax)] = \frac{1}{|a|} F\left(\frac{s}{a}\right), a \ne 0\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Proof: } F[f(ax)] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(ax) e^{i s x} dx\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{Let } u = ax, du = a dx \Rightarrow dx = du/a\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{For } a>0: F[f(ax)] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u) e^{i s (u/a)} \frac{du}{a} = \frac{1}{a} F\left(\frac{s}{a}\right)\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{For } a<0: limits reverse, giving same with } 1/|a|\)

(2 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{State and prove the change of scale property of Fourier transforms.}\)

lq.ANSWER: \(The \quad complex \quad Fourier \quad transform \quad of \quad a \quad function \quad f(x) \quad is \quad defined \quad as \\ F(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)e^{isx}\,dx.\\ Given\\ f(x)= \begin{cases} 1, & -1<x<1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\\ Thus,\\ F(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-1}^{1} e^{isx}\,dx.\\ Now,\\ \int e^{isx}\,dx = \frac{e^{isx}}{is}.\\ Hence,\\ F(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left[\frac{e^{isx}}{is}\right]_{-1}^{1}\\ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{e^{is}-e^{-is}}{is}.\\ Using \quad the \quad identity \quad e^{is}-e^{-is}=2i\sin s,\\ F(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{2i\sin s}{is}\\ = \frac{2\sin s}{s\sqrt{2\pi}}.\\ \boxed{ F(s)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\,\frac{\sin s}{s} }\\ \)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(Find\quad the\quad Fourier\quad transform \quad of \quad the\quad function\\ f(x)= \begin{cases} 1, & |x|<1,\\ 0, & |x|\ge 1. \end{cases} \)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
The Fourier transform of f(x) is defined as:(2)
\(F(s) = \mathcal{F}\{f(x)\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{isx} dx\)(2)
The linearity property states: \(\mathcal{F}\{af(x) + bg(x)\} = a\mathcal{F}\{f(x)\} + b\mathcal{F}\{g(x)\}\)(2)
Proof: \(\mathcal{F}\{af(x)+bg(x)\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} [af(x)+bg(x)]e^{isx}dx\)(2)
\(= a\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)e^{isx}dx + b\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)e^{isx}dx\)(2)
\(= aF(s) + bG(s)\)(2)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Define the Fourier transform of a function \(f(x)\). State and prove the linearity property of Fourier transforms.}\)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
Statement: If \(\mathcal{F}\{f(x)\} = F(s)\), then \(\mathcal{F}\{f(x-a)\} = e^{ias}F(s)\)(2)
Proof: Let \(g(x) = f(x-a)\)(2)
\(G(s) = \mathcal{F}\{g(x)\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x-a) e^{isx} dx\)(2)
Put \(t = x-a\), then \(x = t+a\), \(dx = dt\)(2)
\(G(s) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{is(t+a)} dt = e^{ias} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{ist} dt\)(4)
\(= e^{ias} F(s)\)(3)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{State and prove the shifting property of Fourier transforms: } \mathcal{F}\{f(x-a)\} = e^{ias}F(s).\)
